allEvents.label: grokLiteraryAuthor
allEvents.after:
The elder's hand rose for the warding gesture, his fingers already tracing the first curve of the binding sigil meant to lock the failure in place. I broke the band across my mouth with a sharp twist of my wrist, the leather snapping free so the next words could leave me clear. The accusation the elder had started to form died on his tongue as I spoke the invocation syllable aloud, forcing the final thread of the rite into the open air where any hidden misalignment could be measured.

The family at the canopy's edge surged forward, their voices rising in a single wave of blame. They named me the interference, the one who had stepped between the youth and the elder's seal, the one who had dragged the failed wish upright instead of letting the price claim it cleanly. The elder's eyes narrowed further, the luminous violet of his pupils contracting as he turned the charge back on the youth herself, claiming the grass cooling under my palm could only have come from an ill-wish she had carried into the circle. The crowd's murmurs thickened, some naming Julian again, the one whose alignment-sense never wavered, the one they would call if the rite could not be salvaged without further loss.

I tried to name the twist I felt beneath my palm, the way the grass had shifted from crimson to a dull, resisting brown the moment the youth's voice warped. The words would not arrange themselves. The misalignment was real, the bond between the youth and the wish fraying in a pattern I had never encountered, yet I could offer no cause, no source, no name that would satisfy the circle. My heel pressed harder into the spiralgrass, the blades yielding only enough to show the pressure and no more.

The elder's shadow lengthened across both of us. "The rite is sealed," he said, voice low and final. "Any further interference will be read as defiance of the public safeguard."

The youth's eyes had gone fully translucent, her weight sagging against my grip. I held her upright, my alignment-sense still flaring hot against the sour thread, and the crowd's accusations circled tighter. Someone at the edge called for Julian by name, the syllables carrying the weight of precedent. The elder did not object. He simply waited, his thumb still circled the first sigil line he had drawn.

Julian arrived without announcement, the canopy parting around his presence as though the weave itself had already decided the matter. He moved through the gathered First Favored with the quiet intensity that always made the room feel smaller, his breath stirring the nearest blades of spiralgrass. The slight asymmetry of his mouth tightened when his gaze found the youth's rigid posture and the elder's unfinished sigil. He did not speak at once. His hand turned the signet ring on his finger once, the metal catching the low light that filtered through the willow veil-canopy.

I felt the shift the moment his eyes met mine across the youth's bowed head. The crowd's accusations had not reached him yet, but the tension had. He lowered himself beside me with visible reluctance, his knee knocking once against mine before he steadied it. His palm came to rest on the Alignment Circle etched into the spiralgrass, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him.

The decision pressed against my ribs before he spoke. I could demand the full weight of his alignment-sense, the complete examination that would bind him to the outcome as surely as the wish had bound the youth. Or I could accept the limited reach he offered now, the single hand on the circle, the refusal to commit beyond what the elder's summons required.

Julian's fingers spread across the etched lines. The grass beneath them darkened another shade, the grass cooling another shade under his touch with a slow, reluctant pulse. He did not look at me again. His attention stayed on the circle, the weight of what he was choosing to measure settling between us like another unspoken accusation.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed on it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No — a way in.

I broke the band across my mouth with a sharp twist of my wrist, the leather snapping free so the next words could leave me clear. The accusation the elder had started to form died on his tongue as I spoke the invocation syllable aloud, forcing the final thread of the rite into the open air where any hidden misalignment could be measured.

The family at the canopy's edge surged forward, their voices rising in a single wave of blame. They named me the interference, the one who had stepped between the youth and the elder's seal, the one who had dragged the failed wish upright instead of letting the price claim it cleanly. The elder's eyes narrowed further, the luminous violet of his pupils contracting as he turned the charge back on the youth herself, claiming the grass cooling under my palm could only have come from an ill-wish she had carried into the circle. The crowd's murmurs thickened, some naming Julian again, the one whose alignment-sense never wavered, the one they would call if the rite could not be salvaged without further loss.

I tried to name the twist I felt beneath my palm, the way the grass had shifted from crimson to a dull, resisting brown the moment the youth's voice warped. The words would not arrange themselves. The misalignment was real, the bond between the youth and the wish fraying in a pattern I had never encountered, yet I could offer no cause, no source, no name that would satisfy the circle. My heel pressed harder into the spiralgrass, the blades yielding only enough to show the pressure and no more.

The elder's shadow lengthened across both of us. "The rite is sealed," he said, voice low and final. "Any further interference will be read as defiance of the public safeguard."

The youth's eyes had gone fully translucent, her weight sagging against my grip. I held her upright, my alignment-sense still flaring hot against the sour thread, and the crowd's accusations circled tighter. Someone at the edge called for Julian by name, the syllables carrying the weight of precedent. The elder did not object. He simply waited, his thumb still circled the first sigil line he had drawn.

Julian arrived without announcement, the canopy parting around his presence as though the weave itself had already decided the matter. He moved through the gathered First Favored with the quiet intensity that always made the room feel smaller, his breath stirring the nearest blades of spiralgrass. The slight asymmetry of his mouth tightened when his gaze found the youth's rigid posture and the elder's unfinished sigil. He did not speak at once. His hand turned the signet ring on his finger once, the metal catching the low light that filtered through the willow veil-canopy.

I felt the shift the moment his eyes met mine across the youth's bowed head. The crowd's accusations had not reached him yet, but the tension had. He lowered himself beside me with visible reluctance, his knee knocking once against mine before he steadied it. His palm came to rest on the Alignment Circle etched into the spiralgrass, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him.

The decision pressed against my ribs before he spoke. I could demand the full weight of his alignment-sense, the complete examination that would bind him to the outcome as surely as the wish had bound the youth. Or I could accept the limited reach he offered now, the single hand on the circle, the refusal to commit beyond what the elder's summons required.

Julian's fingers spread across the etched lines. The grass beneath them darkened another shade, the grass cooling another shade under his touch with a slow, reluctant pulse. He did not look at me again. His attention stayed on the circle, the weight of what he was choosing to measure settling between us like another unspoken accusation.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed on it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No — a way in.

allEvents.label: grokLiteraryAuthor
allEvents.after:
The rustling leaves of the willow tree curled around Julian's shoulders, the air beneath them cooling as the branches took the shift. I watched the way the limbs sagged under the afternoon light and felt the same pull along my own spine. The tarot deck in my hand had grown warm against my ribs, the gold edges pressing into my skin through the linen of my shirt. I hadn't realized how much I had been holding my breath until Julian's knee knocked against mine, a low scrape of his boot sole dragged once across the etched line before he settled. A cricket began its steady chirr somewhere under the nearest root, the rhythm matching the pulse I felt in my wrist.

A faint metallic tang rose from the cards where my thumb had worn the gold leaf thinner. *Interference. The one who had stepped between the youth and the elder's seal.* The words settled into the hollow behind my sternum, where the weight of a dozen half-spoken bargains pooled. I flexed my fingers around the deck, the cards shifting against each other with a quiet shush. The cold press of the wood against my palm reminded me of the last time I had held the deck, of the way the cards had slipped out of my grip when the edges caught. *Petition Fate.* The thought settled into my ribs like a promise I wasn't sure I could trust. My thumb traced the edge of the card that had slipped free, the raised gold letters pressing into my skin. *Petition Fate.* As if wishing would be enough.

Julian's other hand settled onto the Alignment Circle, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. A single drop of sweat slid from his temple and vanished into the collar of his shirt before he cleared his throat. One dry leaf detached from the lowest branch and landed on the back of my wrist.

He didn't look at me. His attention stayed fixed on the circle, the weight of what he was choosing to measure settling between us like another unspoken accusation. The elder's shadow lengthened across both of us, the warding gesture still poised in the air. The air between us crackled, the tension so thick it pressed against the space where my hand rested. My heel pressed harder into the spiralgrass, the blades yielding only enough to show the pressure and no more. The dark brown waves swung forward as he leaned in, the long lashes lowering once to shield the sharp angles of his gaze. In the right light, it was the kind of face a camera would have loved and the room already did. The elder's voice still rang in my ears, the accusation sharp enough to cut through the hum of the gathering.

Julian's fingers spread across the etched lines, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. His breath hitched for just a moment, the air thick with unspoken longing, and I felt the shift before he spoke. The way his gaze lingered on my lips before he turned his head, the hesitation in the tilt of his shoulders, the way his fingers twitched as if ready to pull away. The rustling leaves seemed to whisper against my skin, the sound carrying the weight of a decision that hadn't yet been made.

A cricket began its steady chirr somewhere under the nearest root, the rhythm matching the pulse I felt in my wrist.

A faint metallic tang rose from the cards where my thumb had worn the gold leaf thinner. *Interference. The one who had stepped between the youth and the elder's seal.* The words settled into the hollow behind my sternum, where the weight of a dozen half-spoken bargains pooled. I flexed my fingers around the deck, the cards shifting against each other with a quiet shush. The cold press of the wood against my palm reminded me of the last time I had held the deck, of the way the cards had slipped out of my grip when the edges caught. *Petition Fate.* The thought settled into my ribs like a promise I wasn't sure I could trust. My thumb traced the edge of the card that had slipped free, the raised gold letters pressing into my skin. *Petition Fate.* As if wishing would be enough.

Julian's other hand settled onto the Alignment Circle, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. A single drop of sweat slid from his temple and vanished into the collar of his shirt before he cleared his throat. One dry leaf detached from the lowest branch and landed on the back of my wrist.

He didn't look at me. His attention stayed fixed on the circle, the weight of what he was choosing to measure settling between us like another unspoken accusation. The elder's shadow lengthened across both of us, the warding gesture still poised in the air. The air between us crackled, the tension so thick it pressed against the space where my hand rested. My heel pressed harder into the spiralgrass, the blades yielding only enough to show the pressure and no more. My strikingly angular face, softened by long, dark lashes, caught the light as he leaned in, and I could feel the unexpected burst of my laughter reverberate in the space between us. In the right light, it was the kind of face that made a room reset itself by a half-degree. The elder's voice still rang in my ears, the accusation sharp enough to cut through the hum of the gathering.

Julian's fingers spread across the etched lines, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. His breath hitched for just a moment, the air thick with unspoken longing, and I felt the shift before he spoke. The way his gaze lingered on my lips before he turned his head, the hesitation in the tilt of his shoulders, the way his fingers twitched as if ready to pull away. The rustling leaves seemed to whisper against my skin, the sound carrying the weight of a decision that hadn't yet been made.

I flexed my fingers around the deck, the cards shifting against each other with a quiet shush. The cold press of the wood against my palm reminded me of the last time I had held the deck, of the way the cards had slipped out of my grip when the edges caught. *Petition Fate.* The thought settled into my ribs like a promise I wasn't sure I could trust. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. A single drop of sweat slid from his temple and vanished into the collar of his shirt before he cleared his throat. One dry leaf detached from the lowest branch and landed on the back of my wrist.

He didn't look at me. His attention stayed fixed on the circle, the weight of what he was choosing to measure settling between us like another unspoken accusation. The elder's shadow lengthened across both of us, the warding gesture still poised in the air. The air between us crackled, the tension so thick it pressed against the space where my hand rested. My heel pressed harder into the spiralgrass, the blades yielding only enough to show the pressure and no more. My strikingly angular face, softened by long, dark lashes, caught the light as he leaned in, and I could feel the unexpected burst of my laughter reverberate in the space between us. In the right light, it was the kind of face that made a room reset itself by a half-degree. The elder's voice still rang in my ears, the accusation sharp enough to cut through the hum of the gathering.

Julian's fingers spread across the etched lines, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The rustling leaves seemed to whisper against my skin, the sound carrying the weight of a decision that hadn't yet been made.

allEvents.label: grokLiteraryAuthor
allEvents.after:
The rustling leaves of the willow tree held a held-breath stillness, the air under the branches refusing to move. I tilted my head back, letting the dappled light play across my lips, and exhaled against the curve of the deck still warm from my palm. The card beneath my thumb shifted—Petition Fate. The ink at the bottom edge glinted faintly, the edge of the card catching the light as if the paper had shifted. I didn’t pull my hand away. Not yet.

Julian’s shadow fell across my boots before I heard him. The willow branches bent where he passed, the motion arriving with him. He stood half a stride away, his stance casual but his knuckles white where they gripped the Alignment Circle etched into the spiralgrass. The sigil under his palm pulsed once, a slow current of violet light bleeding from the lines into the soil. He didn’t look at me. His gaze stayed fixed on the circle, his breath measured, the count of seconds audible in the pause before he could lift his hand.

“You’re still here,” he said, voice low and deliberate. The words weren’t an accusation, but they weren’t kindness either. They landed between us as a challenge.

I wrapped my fingers around the deck, the gold edges biting into my skin. “You’re the one who hasn’t left.”

His mouth twisted, not quite a smile. The gap between his front teeth showed for a fraction of a second, then vanished under the neutral set of his jaw. The ring clicked once against his knuckle, the sound thin against the grass. “Alignment-sense tells me the bond is fraying faster than it should. The elder claims it’s the youth’s fault. I say it’s the elder’s design.” His fingers flexed against the circle, the spiralgrass darkening where pressure met the lines. “Either way, the circle won’t last another turning without intervention.”

I shifted my weight, the tarot deck pressing harder against my ribs. “Intervention requires two hands.”

Julian’s eyes flickered toward me then, a faint scar at the corner of his left eye pulling tighter. They narrowed just enough to register the invitation. “Intervention requires trust,” he said. “And I haven’t decided you’re worth the risk.”

The air between us thickened, the willow’s rustling rising as the branches shifted overhead. My fingers twitched against the deck. I could feel the weight of the alignment issue pressing against my ribs, the elder’s life force bleeding into the earth beneath us. But it wasn’t the crisis that made my breath stutter. It was the way Julian’s gaze lingered on the curve of my throat, the way his fingers curled slightly against the circle as if holding back from reaching for me instead.

He exhaled sharply; a dry leaf skittered across the spiralgrass between us. “Fine,” he said. “But it’s your fault if the circle breaks.” His hand turned the ring again, the metal catching the light one last time before he pressed the other palm to the Alignment Circle. The sigil flared white-hot for a heartbeat, the spiralgrass hissing beneath the heat.

I didn’t look away. I couldn’t. Not when the circle pulsed again, not when the ground trembled beneath us, not when Julian’s heel scraped once against the spiralgrass. The alignment-sense flared against my ribs, the pressure of it pressing against the back of my teeth, but I didn’t break the gaze. Not when the circle flared, not when the branches above answered with their own shift, not when the deck in my hand warmed like a living thing.

Petition Fate. The thought flickered through me, small and desperate. One ask. One small thing to tip the scales back in our favor.

I realize the deck is still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds (or maybe arcing up?) Ow! Static shock reminds me I need to pay attention to the present...

His mouth twisted, not quite a smile. The gap between his front teeth showed for a fraction of a second, then vanished under the neutral set of his jaw. The ring clicked once against his knuckle, the sound thin against the grass. “Alignment-sense tells me the bond is fraying faster than it should. The elder claims it’s the youth’s fault. I say it’s the elder’s design.” His fingers flexed against the circle, the spiralgrass darkening where pressure met the lines. “Either way, the circle won’t last another turning without intervention.”

I shifted my weight, the tarot deck pressing harder against my ribs. “Intervention requires two hands.”

Julian’s eyes flickered toward me then, a faint scar at the corner of his left eye pulling tighter. They narrowed just enough to register the invitation. “Intervention requires trust,” he said. “And I haven’t decided you’re worth the risk.”

The air between us thickened, the willow’s rustling rising as the branches shifted overhead. My fingers twitched against the deck. I could feel the weight of the alignment issue pressing against my ribs, the elder’s life force bleeding into the earth beneath us. But it wasn’t the crisis that made my breath stutter. It was the way Julian’s gaze lingered on the curve of my throat, the way his fingers curled slightly against the circle as if holding back from reaching for me instead.

He exhaled sharply; a dry leaf skittered across the spiralgrass between us. “Fine,” he said. “But it’s your fault if the circle breaks.” His hand turned the ring again, the metal catching the light one last time before he pressed the other palm to the Alignment Circle. The sigil flared white-hot for a heartbeat, the spiralgrass hissing beneath the heat.

I didn’t look away. I couldn’t. Not when the circle pulsed again, not when the ground trembled beneath us, not when Julian’s heel scraped once against the spiralgrass. The alignment-sense flared against my ribs, the pressure of it pressing against the back of my teeth, but I didn’t break the gaze. Not when the circle flared, not when the branches above answered with their own shift, not when the deck in my hand warmed like a living thing.

Petition Fate. The thought flickered through me, small and desperate. One ask. One small thing to tip the scales back in our favor.

I realize the deck is still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds (or maybe arcing up?) Ow! Static shock reminds me I need to pay attention to the present...

The ink at the bottom edge glinted faintly, the edge of the card catching the light as if the paper had shifted. I didn’t pull my hand away. Not yet.

Julian’s shadow fell across my boots before I heard him. The willow branches bent where he passed, the motion arriving with him. He stood half a stride away, his stance casual but his knuckles white where they gripped the Alignment Circle etched into the spiralgrass. The sigil under his palm pulsed once, a slow current of violet light bleeding from the lines into the soil. He didn’t look at me. His gaze stayed fixed on the circle, his breath measured, the count of seconds audible in the pause before he could lift his hand.

“You’re still here,” he said, voice low and deliberate. The words weren’t an accusation, but they weren’t kindness either. They landed between us as a challenge.

I wrapped my fingers around the deck, the gold edges biting into my skin. “You’re the one who hasn’t left.”

His mouth twisted, not quite a smile. The gap between his front teeth showed for a fraction of a second, then vanished under the neutral set of his jaw. The ring clicked once against his knuckle, the sound thin against the grass. “Alignment-sense tells me the bond is fraying faster than it should. The elder claims it’s the youth’s fault. I say it’s the elder’s design.” His fingers flexed against the circle, the spiralgrass darkening where pressure met the lines. “Either way, the circle won’t last another turning without intervention.”

I shifted my weight, the tarot deck pressing harder against my ribs. “Intervention requires two hands.”

Julian’s eyes flickered toward me then, a faint scar at the corner of his left eye pulling tighter. They narrowed just enough to register the invitation. “Intervention requires trust,” he said. “And I haven’t decided you’re worth the risk.”

The air between us thickened, the willow’s rustling rising as the branches shifted overhead. My fingers twitched against the deck. I could feel the weight of the alignment issue pressing against my ribs, the elder’s life force bleeding into the earth beneath us. But it wasn’t the crisis that made my breath stutter. It was the way Julian’s gaze lingered on the curve of my throat, the way his fingers curled slightly against the circle as if holding back from reaching for me instead.

He exhaled sharply; a dry leaf skittered across the spiralgrass between us. “Fine,” he said. “But it’s your fault if the circle breaks.” His hand turned the ring again, the metal catching the light one last time before he pressed the other palm to the Alignment Circle. The sigil flared white-hot for a heartbeat, the spiralgrass hissing beneath the heat.

I didn’t look away. I couldn’t. Not when the circle pulsed again, not when the ground trembled beneath us, not when Julian’s heel scraped once against the spiralgrass. The alignment-sense flared against my ribs, the pressure of it pressing against the back of my teeth, but I didn’t break the gaze. Not when the circle flared, not when the branches above answered with their own shift, not when the deck in my hand warmed like a living thing.

Petition Fate. The thought flickered through me, small and desperate. One ask. One small thing to tip the scales back in our favor.

I realize the deck is still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds (or maybe arcing up?) Ow! Static shock reminds me I need to pay attention to the present...

I tilted my head back, letting the dappled light play across my lips, and exhaled against the curve of the deck still warm from my palm. The card beneath my thumb shifted—Petition Fate. The ink at the bottom edge glinted faintly, as though the words themselves had leaned closer to the edge. I didn’t pull my hand away. Not yet.

Julian’s shadow fell across my boots before I heard him. The willow branches bent under the weight of his presence, as if they’d been waiting for him to arrive. He stood half a stride away, his stance casual but his knuckles white where they gripped the Alignment Circle etched into the spiralgrass. The sigil under his palm pulsed once, a slow current of violet light bleeding from the lines into the soil. He didn’t look at me. His gaze stayed fixed on the circle, his breath measured, as though he were counting the seconds until he could pull his hand back and be rid of it.

“You’re still here,” he said, voice low and deliberate. The words weren’t an accusation, but they weren’t kindness either. They were a challenge wrapped in the shape of a statement.

I wrapped my fingers around the deck, the gold edges biting into my skin. “You’re the one who hasn’t left.”

His mouth twisted, not quite a smile. The gap between his front teeth showed for a fraction of a second, sharp and deliberate, like he’d rehearsed the imperfection. Then it was gone, swallowed by the careful neutrality he wore like armor. He turned the signet ring on his finger once, the metal catching the filtered light. “Alignment-sense tells me the bond is fraying faster than it should. The elder claims it’s the youth’s fault. I say it’s the elder’s design.” His fingers flexed against the circle, the spiralgrass darkening where he touched it, as though the ground itself recoiled. “Either way, the circle won’t last another turning without intervention.”

I shifted my weight, the tarot deck pressing harder against my ribs. “Intervention requires two hands.”

Julian’s eyes flickered toward me then, his irises shifting between forest green and cool sea-gray like the tide caught between two moons. They narrowed just enough to let me know he’d registered the invitation in my words. “Intervention requires trust,” he said. “And I haven’t decided you’re worth the risk.”

The air between us thickened, the willow’s rustling growing louder, as though the tree itself had leaned in to listen. My fingers twitched against the deck. I could feel the weight of the alignment issue pressing against my ribs, the mentor’s life force bleeding into the earth beneath us. But it wasn’t the crisis that made my breath stutter. It was the way Julian’s gaze lingered on the curve of my throat, the way his fingers curled slightly against the circle as if holding back from reaching for me instead.

He exhaled sharply, the breath hitching for a single impossible moment, the air between us thickening with something unspoken. “Fine,” he said. “But it’s your fault if the circle breaks.” His hand turned the ring again, the metal catching the light one last time before he pressed the other palm to the Alignment Circle. The sigil flared white-hot for a heartbeat, the spiralgrass hissing beneath the heat.

I didn’t look away. I couldn’t. Not when the circle pulsed again, not when the ground trembled beneath us, not when Julian’s breath hitched once more, his gaze locked on mine with an intensity that made the world around us feel smaller. I tilted my head back, letting the dappled light play across my lips, and exhaled against the curve of the deck still warm from my palm. The card beneath my thumb shifted—Petition Fate. The ink at the bottom edge glinted faintly, the edge of the card catching the light as if the paper had shifted. I didn’t pull my hand away. Not yet.

Julian’s shadow fell across my boots before I heard him. The willow branches bent where he passed, the motion arriving with him. He stood half a stride away, his stance casual but his knuckles white where they gripped the Alignment Circle etched into the spiralgrass. The sigil under his palm pulsed once, a slow current of violet light bleeding from the lines into the soil. He didn’t look at me. His gaze stayed fixed on the circle, his breath measured, the count of seconds audible in the pause before he could lift his hand.

“You’re still here,” he said, voice low and deliberate. The words weren’t an accusation, but they weren’t kindness either. They landed between us as a challenge.

I wrapped my fingers around the deck, the gold edges biting into my skin. “You’re the one who hasn’t left.”

His mouth twisted, not quite a smile. The gap between his front teeth showed for a fraction of a second, then vanished under the neutral set of his jaw. The ring clicked once against his knuckle, the sound thin against the grass. “Alignment-sense tells me the bond is fraying faster than it should. The elder claims it’s the youth’s fault. I say it’s the elder’s design.” His fingers flexed against the circle, the spiralgrass darkening where pressure met the lines. “Either way, the circle won’t last another turning without intervention.”

Julian’s eyes flickered toward me then, a faint scar at the corner of his left eye pulling tighter. They narrowed just enough to register the invitation. “Intervention requires trust,” he said. “And I haven’t decided you’re worth the risk.”

The air between us thickened, the willow’s rustling rising as the branches shifted overhead. My fingers twitched against the deck. I could feel the weight of the alignment issue pressing against my ribs, the elder’s life force bleeding into the earth beneath us. But it wasn’t the crisis that made my breath stutter. It was the way Julian’s gaze lingered on the curve of my throat, the way his fingers curled slightly against the circle as if holding back from reaching for me instead.

checkpoints.label: window._authorChatCapture
checkpoints.text:
The rustling leaves of the willow tree curled around Julian's shoulders, the air beneath them cooling as the branches took the shift. I watched the way the limbs sagged under the afternoon light and felt the same pull along my own spine. The tarot deck in my hand had grown warm against my ribs, the gold edges pressing into my skin through the linen of my shirt. I hadn't realized how much I had been holding my breath until Julian's knee knocked against mine, a low scrape of his boot sole dragged once across the etched line before he settled. A cricket began its steady chirr somewhere under the nearest root, the rhythm matching the pulse I felt in my wrist.

A faint metallic tang rose from the cards where my thumb had worn the gold leaf thinner. *Interference. The one who had stepped between the youth and the elder's seal.* The words settled into the hollow behind my sternum, where the weight of a dozen half-spoken bargains pooled. I flexed my fingers around the deck, the cards shifting against each other with a quiet shush. The cold press of the wood against my palm reminded me of the last time I had held the deck, of the way the cards had slipped out of my grip when the edges caught. *Petition Fate.* The thought settled into my ribs like a promise I wasn't sure I could trust. My thumb traced the edge of the card that had slipped free, the raised gold letters pressing into my skin. *Petition Fate.* As if wishing would be enough.

Julian's other hand settled onto the Alignment Circle, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. A single drop of sweat slid from his temple and vanished into the collar of his shirt before he cleared his throat. One dry leaf detached from the lowest branch and landed on the back of my wrist.

He didn't look at me. His attention stayed fixed on the circle, the weight of what he was choosing to measure settling between us like another unspoken accusation. The elder's shadow lengthened across both of us, the warding gesture still poised in the air. The air between us crackled, the tension so thick it pressed against the space where my hand rested. My heel pressed harder into the spiralgrass, the blades yielding only enough to show the pressure and no more. The dark brown waves swung forward as he leaned in, the long lashes lowering once to shield the sharp angles of his gaze. In the right light, it was the kind of face a camera would have loved and the room already did. The elder's voice still rang in my ears, the accusation sharp enough to cut through the hum of the gathering.

Julian's fingers spread across the etched lines, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. His breath hitched for just a moment, the air thick with unspoken longing, and I felt the shift before he spoke. The way his gaze lingered on my lips before he turned his head, the hesitation in the tilt of his shoulders, the way his fingers twitched as if ready to pull away. The rustling leaves seemed to whisper against my skin, the sound carrying the weight of a decision that hadn't yet been made.

“Either way, the circle won’t last another turning without intervention.”

I shifted my weight, the tarot deck pressing harder against my ribs.

“Intervention requires two hands.”

Julian’s eyes flickered toward me then, a faint scar at the corner of his left eye pulling tighter. They narrowed just enough to register the invitation.

“Intervention requires trust,” he said.

“And I haven’t decided you’re worth the risk.”

The air between us thickened, the willow’s rustling rising as the branches shifted overhead. My fingers twitched against the deck. I could feel the weight of the alignment issue pressing against my ribs, the elder’s life force bleeding into the earth beneath us. But it wasn’t the crisis that made my breath stutter. It was the way Julian’s gaze lingered on the curve of my throat, the way his fingers curled slightly against the circle as if holding back from reaching for me instead. He exhaled sharply; a dry leaf skittered across the spiralgrass between us.

“Fine,” he said.

“But it’s your fault if the circle breaks.”

His hand turned the ring again, the metal catching the light one last time before he pressed the other palm to the Alignment Circle. The sigil flared white-hot for a heartbeat, the spiralgrass hissing beneath the heat. I didn’t look away. I couldn’t. Not when the circle pulsed again, not when the ground trembled beneath us, not when Julian’s heel scraped once against the spiralgrass. The alignment-sense flared against my ribs, the pressure of it pressing against the back of my teeth, but I didn’t break the gaze. Not when the circle flared, not when the branches above answered with their own shift, not when the deck in my hand warmed like a living thing. Petition Fate. The thought flickered through me, small and desperate. One ask. One small thing to tip the scales back in our favor.

“Tempt Fate.”

Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds (or maybe arcing up?) Ow! Static shock reminds me I need to pay attention to the present…

I realize the deck is still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Grandma never let me play with that one.
